articles.headline: Ohio Election.
articles.text: The latest returns from Ohio indicate a majority of at least 12,000 for the Republicans. This result is especially discouraging to the Democrats, as they were basing great hopes on the moral effect of a victory in Ohio. The Republicans are correspondingly elated and everything now looks propitious for a Republican victory in November. Our next issue will contain the full report. West Virginia, as was expected, went Democratic.
articles.summary: Reports Republican majority of at least 12,000 in the Ohio election and that West Virginia went Democratic.

articles.headline: M. S. & F. Co.
articles.text:
Nineteen passengers the first week is a very creditable showing for the new stage line, as it has not been advertised as yet. The start was made a little too late to catch the bulk of the fall trade, but we learned in the Hills that we are sure to get the most of the out-going travel at least. Everyone wishes to try the new line, and this is all the proprietors wish. No one is going to undergo the tedious and uncomfortable stage journey on the other lines, which take two nights or more, when by our line only one night is spent in the stage. Our road-bed is already far superior to that of the other lines and from fifteen to eighty miles shorter.

The N. P. Express Co. has already made arrangements to carry and deliver express matter to all points in the Hills. This is an advantage possessed by no other stage line terminating in the Hills country. Through rates to all points can be quoted, and we are assured that the bulk of the express matter will come our way. The same rates as by the other roads are also made for passengers. The Northern Pacific being the road which broke the monopoly held by the Pierre lines, has a warm place in the hearts of the Hillers, and as freight will be carried at the same rates, there is no question that a large quantity will continue to arrive at this point for the Hills.

The line is now in good working order, but improvements will constantly be made. Everything that conduces to the comfort of passengers will especially oe added and the line must be pronounced the best going into the Hills.

If the present rate of travel is any criterion of what will be required when it is thoroughly advertised, a daily will be put on in the spring at least. At any rate one will be put on as soon as it is required.

We have never seen such perfect unanimity as is that of the Black Hills people in wishing our line every success. It opens a new country that can be easily reached, instead of travelling several more days by stage and railroad. For instance, it brings Bismarck a thousand miles nearer than via Pierre and St. Paul, and to points west the distance is lessened still more.

The M. S. & F. Co. has come here to stay, and we wish to prophesy right now is only the advance guard of a railroad from here to the Hills.
articles.summary: The new Medora-Black Hills stage line (M. S. & F. Co.) carried nineteen passengers its first week; the N. P. Express Co. will route Hills express by it, and a daily line is promised.

articles.text: A subject of which we have never written editorially, and concerning which all argument is wasted, was brought to our notice by seeing in the Mandan Pioneer a notice of the "Billings county convention." This convention was held at Belfield, October 11, and elected Messrs. Blankenberg and Harbison as delegates. In the minutes of the convention there were only three names mentioned, and from one of the participants we learn that those attending did not greatly exceed this number. In any event their meeting was unauthorized, and they capped the climax by advocating the very plan that would be a death-blow to the future of Billings county—its still further division at some point a few miles west of Fryburg. In the event of such an impossibility taking place as this division, we would like to have the citizens of Belfield who attended the meeting rise up and explain where the property is to pay taxes for a a county organization for the eastern half. This is a subject that we have not before mentioned, but it is a fact that when the county is organized, the western half will for a long time have to support the eastern half. There is fifty dollars west of Fryburg to one east of it. In the light of this statement it looks a good deal like an exaggerated case of the tail wagging the dog for the eastern part of the county to try and dictate terms to the western part. For no other reason than that of blind jealousy, a few embryonic politicians in Belfield who should still be wearing swaddling clothes, have posed as marplots until patience has ceased to be a virtue. These few remind one of the tailors of Tuley street, who issued a manifesto beginning, "We, the citizens of Great Britain." They do not represent the citizens of Belfield, as we know from actual conversations. They do not represent the people of Billings county, as men and not babies must do that. All they represent is their own pitiably insignificent selves. It is time the people of Belfield stopped following such leaders and chose for themselves such captains as would come to the front and, even after one disastrous defeat, lead on instead of putting up cats' paws to be burned getting their chestnuts out of the fire. In all the conventions held at Medora, Belfield has received its share and more than its share. In the so-called Belfield conventions, Medora has never even been mentioned, except as to means for her defeat. Like the dog going across the stream with the huge chunk of meat in its mouth, and seeing its reflection below, dropped his original piece in grasping after the shadow, Belfield will get "heap nothing" if it pursues its present porcine policy.
articles.summary: Editorial denouncing the unauthorized "Billings county convention" held at Belfield October 11 and its proposal to divide the county west of Fryburg.

articles.headline: STOCK NOTES.
articles.text:
Prices on the Chicago markets have been a little less encouraging this week.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

During Thursday and Friday last cattle shipments aggregated 12,656 head. This is the largest total for any two consecutive days in the history of the trade.—[Breeder's Gazette.

Range cattle continue to arrive at the rate of from 5,000 to 7,000 head per day, but all are promptly taken, local canners and dressed-beef shippers being the principal buyers.—[Breeder's Gazette.

We can supply the world with the best of meat. A second order for 50,000 pounds of compressed beef for the British expedition to Kartoum has been given to a Chicago firm.—[Col. L. S. Record.

Imported cattle haue been distributed through all portions of the country. So far the Short-horns lead any other breed as to numbers, but the Herefords and Polled-Angus are now moving strong. These leading breeds are now found scattered all over the country from Texas to Montana.

The cattle thieves and six-shooter ex-deputy sheriffs, who have so long held sway here, terrorizing quiet citizens and depredating upon the herds of legitimate stockmen, now appear as very ordinary individuals, and are actually seen in court playing the humiliating role of defendant in cases of theft of cattle. How the mighty have fallen.—[Henriette (Tex.) Shield.

The stock interests in Colorado and Wyoming are growing, and great difficulty is found in getting range. In talking with a number of the leading ranchmen, we were surprised to find the loss from last winter so small, many of them expressing great wonder at it themselves; but the round-up has shown a very healthy condition of stock, as well as small loss.—[Nebraska Farmer.

An exchange says that if the stockmen in the pastoral region of the United States, from New Mexico to the British possessions, desire to have the homestead law enlarged to four sections, they can accomplish this result simply by acting in unison and making the request. A general request accompanied by a complete exhibit of the situation to congress, will accomplish the desired end.

The treatment of all injuries of the foot must be conducted on the same general principles. We must remember that the hoof, its horny covering, is of the nature of a closed box, which will not expand and accommodate itself correspondingly with the swollen and inflamed structures that it incloses and protects. Any person who may have suffered from a "whitlow" beneath the finger-nail can only form a slight idea of the agony experienced by the poor horse suffering from inflammation and suppuration within the hoof. The elasticity of the insensible horn of the sole or frog usually closes the opening through which the injury has been inflicted, and there is no outlet for the pus or matter formed, the result of the inflammation, except at the coronet or above the horn at the heels. The original opening must, therefore, be searched for, the sole or frog well thinned around it, and a good and free orifice made, so that the matter can be freely discharged as it is formed, and the foot then placed in a warm bran poultice, till the inflammation has subsided and the discharge ceased.—[National Live-Stock Journal, Chicago.

Reports say that the Utes are still playing their cuteness in the northwest, and are making times very troublesome for the stockmen holding on those ranges. The cattlemen had quite a skirmish with them not long since, in which one Indian and a number of horses on both sides were killed. It is said that cattle are being gathered with cavalry escort, and further outbreaks from the Utes and Navajos are feared by cattlemen.—[Cheyenne (I. T.) Transporter.

Of all the seasons of the year, from now on and for sixty days the cattle upon the range wil put on the most substantial flesh. The nights are cool, and the quality of the grass is exactly what it should be. The frost has checked its growth, and what the animal now takes of it into its stomach has the substance to produce fat and marbled meat. Those who hurry the bullock away to market now lose the two most valuable months in the year.—[Col. L. S. Record.

In regard to the number of cattle driven out of Texas, a correspondent writing from Doan's Store, at Red river crossing of the Dodge City trail, says that up to a recent date there have crossed at that place 153 herds, containing 394,227 head, not counting horses. He has kept a record since '72, and says the smallest drive over this trail was in ['70?], when only 110,000 head crossed, and the largest in '82, when 415,000 crossed. This alludes to the drive over the Dodge trail alone.—[Col. L. S. Record.

T. J. McMinn, formerly attached to the St. Louis Globe-Democrat, spent last Tuesday in our city. Mr. McMinn is making the tour of the western range country to see how many cattlemen are likely to visit St. Louis at the time of the National convention, Nov. 17th next. He reports the boys all along the line in earnest as to the imporance of the meeting and thinks "our folks" will go down to the city by the river, in vast numbers. We are satisfied that he is correct in his views, for we know of hundreds who have expressed a full determination to go. The good people of St. Louis are making great efforts to render the visit of the stock-growers a pleasant and memorable one and they certainly will succeed in so doing. Wyoming will go a hundred strong and Colorado will do as well. Utah, Idaho, Nevada, Dakota, and Moatana will send large numbers, and we are going prepared to do good to ourselves and try to do good to our neighbors.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

Among the important matters which will be likely to come before the Convention of cattle-growers to be held in this city November 13th will be a proposition for the federal goverment to open a national "trail" from the northwestern boundry of Texas through western Kansas, Colorado, Wyoming and Montana to the British possessions on the north. Such a trail it is proposed to make five miles in width, and as it will involve the donation of an immense amount of the public domain, and a large appropriation of public money to purchase private lands within its proposed lines, it is a matter of great importance to the whole country, which we are satisfied will not be conceded unless the necessity for it is shown to be great. Its object is to afford the breeders of Texas an outlet for their cattle towards the northwest of which they can at no time in the future be deprived. But we understand it is not desired by the Texas people alone, also by the people residing in the territories through which the proposed trail will be laid. These people, it is said, desire convenient opportunity for the purchase of the surplus cattle of Texas, not being so situated as to be able to breed cattle in sufficient numbers to keep their ranges as well stocked as they desire.—[Breeder's Gazette.

Already the prairie fires are beginning to appear, and it will not be many weeks until they can be seen raging on every hand. Every caution should be taken to prevent as far as possible the burning off of the ranges. At this season of the year the grass, parched by the hot sun during the late dry spell, is ready to blaze in a moment if ignited by the least spark, which is often borne on the wind from some camp fire. As a rule, freighters are more careless than anyone else, and, as much as they have been cautioned by the Indians and cattlemen, it is from their camps that the majority of our prairie fires originate. Of course it would not be reasonable to suppose that anyone could maliciously set fire to the grass; but some people, not being interested, are simply careless, who go about without sufficient presence of mind to be careful with their camp fires and to see that every spark is extinguished when leaving a camp. Last fall, a little later than this, a considerable portion of our best ranges were burned, consequently stock of all kinds died from starvation in large numbers, stock-owners suffering heavy losses. Whom shall we blame? Some laid it to the hands of Indians, but it is not reasonable to think that Indians, while directly interested in behalf of their own stock, would be guilty of such work; yet others say that it is a difficult task to "break an old dog of old tricks." Let it be as it may have been, this fall everyone should take the matter in hand and burn fire-guards around his range, making himself safe from the sweeping fires, from whatsoever source they may originate. Only a few fires so far this season have broken out, and it is to be hoped that the ranges will be saved.—[Cheyenne (I. T.) Transporter.
articles.summary: Column of cattle and range notes clipped from stock journals: markets, Texas trail drives, the St. Louis cattlemen's convention, a proposed national cattle trail, hoof care and prairie-fire warnings.

articles.text: The church is rapidly nearing completion.
articles.summary: Medora's new church is nearly complete.

articles.text: Rassie Deffebach will return from the Hills in a few days.
articles.summary: Rassie Deffebach expected back from the Hills.

articles.text: The Marquis returned last evening in his car, Livingston.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Mores returned in his private car, Livingston.

articles.text: Peter Book returned from a short visit to Mandan last evening.
articles.summary: Peter Book returned from Mandan.

articles.text: Mr. B. Barr returned from the Big Horn region this morning.
articles.summary: B. Barr returned from the Big Horn region.

articles.text: Rev. R. H. Dolliver and W. E. Adams were passengers on yesterday's coach going to Deadwood.
articles.summary: Rev. R. H. Dolliver and W. E. Adams left on the stage for Deadwood.

articles.text: Howard Eaton received a number of high grade short horn bulls last Sunday from Pennsylvania.
articles.summary: Howard Eaton received high grade short horn bulls from Pennsylvania.

articles.text: Bob Roberts has completed a large beer cellar which he will fill immediately with his winter's stock.
articles.summary: Bob Roberts completed a large beer cellar.

articles.text: Notice is hereby given that the new church will be blessed the first Sunday in November by Rev. Father Martin.
articles.summary: The new church will be blessed the first Sunday in November by Father Martin.

articles.text: The brick dwelling that is building for J. R. Grymes will afford a very comfortable bachelor home for the residents.
articles.summary: A brick dwelling is being built for J. R. Grymes.

articles.text: There is a well-authenticated rumor that two horse-thieves were hung last night near Glendive. Let the good work go on.
articles.summary: Rumor that two horse-thieves were hanged near Glendive.

articles.text: J. C. Fisher, local manager of the M. S. & F. Co., is in Bismarck attending the legislative convention to which he is a delegate.
articles.summary: J. C. Fisher of the M. S. & F. Co. is a delegate to the legislative convention at Bismarck.

articles.text: Cortez Fessenden, of Huron, surveyor general of Dakota, was a passenger on Saturday's stage from Deadwood, and is on his way to Portland.
articles.summary: Surveyor General Cortez Fessenden passed through on the stage from Deadwood.

articles.text: Johnny Keifer and wife started for St. Paul the first of the week, where they will remain for some time for the benefit of Mrs. Keifer's health.
articles.summary: Johnny Keifer and wife went to St. Paul for Mrs. Keifer's health.

articles.text: Again we can breathe freely for the safety of our property. The band of Gros Ventres Indians have left us, it is to be hoped, never to return.
articles.summary: A band of Gros Ventres Indians has left the Medora area.

articles.text: W. J. Hornbeck, of Lead City, came up on the coach Tuesday evening and went to Billings Wednesday. He expects to pass the winter in Butte City.
articles.summary: W. J. Hornbeck of Lead City came by coach and went on to Billings.

articles.text: Miss Josie Smith, sister-in-law of Rassie Deffebach, came from the Hills on last Saturday evening. She will stay all winter visiting Mrs. Deffebach.
articles.summary: Miss Josie Smith arrived from the Hills to winter with the Deffebachs.

articles.text: F. E. Bowen, one of Mandan's rising attorney's, was in Medora a few days ago on business. He will be an early passenger to the Hills via the stage line.
articles.summary: Mandan attorney F. E. Bowen visited Medora on business.

articles.text: We have been running off so much job work lately that our press finally got disgusted and "busted" on us. We will be ready for another rush in a day or two.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy's press broke down from heavy job work.

articles.text: Miss H. R. Mead arrived from Dickinson this morning and will tomorrow open for business at the Pyramid Prrk hotel, for everything in the millinery line.
articles.summary: Miss H. R. Mead arrived from Dickinson to open a millinery business at the Pyramid Park hotel.

articles.text: From the rustling ability of Messrs. Field, Roberts, Smith and Paddock we can rest assured that the Bad Lands will be well represented at the New Orleans exposition.
articles.summary: Messrs. Field, Roberts, Smith and Paddock gathering Bad Lands exhibits for the New Orleans exposition.

articles.text: Vic Smith has been killing game to be stuffed for the New Orleans exposition, and some of his victims are beauties, especially some mountain sheep that he brought in yesterday.
articles.summary: Vic Smith is killing game, including mountain sheep, to be mounted for the New Orleans exposition.

articles.text: Work has already begun on the new slaughter house, but there has been a change in the plans and work was stopped. To-morrow or next day work will be again resumed.
articles.summary: Work on the new slaughter house began, was stopped for a change of plans, and will resume.

articles.text: Owing to the absence of Mr. Fisher we cannot give the amount of freight forwarded last week. It amounts to 30,000 pounds, and is destined to Spearfish, Deadwood and Lead City.
articles.summary: About 30,000 pounds of freight went by the stage line to the Hills last week.

articles.text: William is mourning in sackcloth and ashes for the loss of all but one of his carrier pigeons. It is to be hoped that they will return, as they bid fair to afford ready and swift connection with the Hills.
articles.summary: William lost all but one of his carrier pigeons intended for messages to the Hills.

articles.text: Proofs of the hangers for the Medora S. & F. Co. have arrived, and they are truly works of art. They were made under the supervision of Mr. J. W. Hornick, of the Pioneer Press, and are as fine pieces of work as the P. P. has ever turned out.
articles.summary: Advertising hangers for the Medora S. & F. Co. arrived from the Pioneer Press.

articles.text: The burning coal mine in the butte east of Medora is already a dangerous rival to the famous burning mine south-west of here. In the night the flames light up the whole butte, and it is a sight well worth seeing. After a look at it one is forced to admit that the description of the Bad Lands "looking like h—l with the fire put out," is rather inadequate.
articles.summary: A burning coal mine in the butte east of Medora lights up the butte at night.

articles.text: The coal mine tunnel is now about ninety feet in, and the quality of the coal is constantly improving. It is undoubtedly the best coal yet discovered in northern Dakota. Provided low enough rates can be secured, a side track will be built and the coal shipped down the road. Orders for local consumption will be immediately filled by leaving directions at this office.
articles.summary: The coal mine tunnel is about ninety feet in; a side track is planned if rates allow.

articles.text: Rev. Father Martin, of Mandan, was in town Tuesday. He reports that the foundation work has begun on his hospital building and that he has every confidence the money will be easily raised for its completion. He made arrangements for a dance to be held here soon at George Fitzgerald's, the proceeds of which will go to the hospital. It is a worthy object and should receive every encouragement.
articles.summary: Father Martin of Mandan reports work begun on his hospital and plans a benefit dance at George Fitzgerald's.

articles.text: The new drug store is fairly under way, and when the stock is all in we can boast of the best drug store between Mandan and Glendive. Dr. Jorgens, the proprietor, is still in Spearfish, but will be here in less than a week. Mr. Martin, the doctor's father-in-law, attends to to the business now, and is an experienced druggist as well as the doctor. We bespeak for the new store the hearty patronage it deserves.
articles.summary: Dr. H. M. Jorgens' new drug store is opening, with his father-in-law Mr. Martin in charge.

articles.text: Miss H. R. Mead, of H. R. Mead & Co., of Bismarck, dealers in dry goods, cloaks, notions, trimmings, fine millinery and hair goods, will open up a full line of notions, trimmings, corsets, gloves, ladies' underwear, wraps, children's and infants' goods, millinery and hair goods, etc., Friday, October 17, at Pyramid Park hotel parlors. The ladies of Medora and and Little Missouri are cordially invited to inspect these goods.
articles.summary: H. R. Mead & Co. of Bismarck will show millinery and dry goods at the Pyramid Park hotel parlors on Friday, October 17.

articles.text: Mr. Field, sub-commisssioner of Dakota to the New Orleans worlds fair, is here rustling specimens and curiosities. It nearly broke our heart to part with the magnificent petrifaction Mr. McGregor gave us, but we could not resist Bob's persuasive eloquence. Our avowed object in getting up this collection was for just such an exhibition as this, but we find that each specimen is coupled with such pleasant recollections of its donor that it is hard to give even one of them up.
articles.summary: Mr. Field, Dakota sub-commissioner to the New Orleans fair, collected specimens in Medora, including a petrifaction from the Cow Boy's collection.

articles.text:
Drugs and Medicines — Dr. H. M. Jorgens, Medora, Dak.; complete stock on the corner of Third avenue and Third street.
Mayville Stock Farm, Mayville, Traill Co., Dak. — The Mayville Herd of Short Horns; J. L. & E. B. Grandin, Props.; W. W. Warren, General Manager.
Hardware and Tinware at J. D. Garver's, Little Missouri, Dak. — all kinds of tin and sheet-iron articles.
Northern Pacific Railroad — "Going East—Going West, Northern Pacific Railroad is your line"; St. Paul to Portland, Ore., Yellowstone National Park; Chas. S. Fee, General Passenger Agent.
Brick!! made at the Medora Brick Kiln — "Guaranteed better than any brick made in Dakota, or money refunded. Only $8 per thousand!"; Peter J. Book, Medora, Dak.
Lots! Lots in Medora — table of blocks, lots and prices; "For sale at the office of the Bad Lands Cow Boy"; A. T. Packard, Medora, Dak.
Beef Cattle — N. P. Ref. Car Co., Medora, Dak., offers its herd of about 700 she cattle and 250 steers (American cattle) and 65 bulls and 55 she cattle (graded), ranged on Beaver creek, Dawson county, Montana, ten miles north of Keith.
Medora Stage & F. Co., A. T. Packard, General Manager, Medora — supply depot; horses strung on stage stations between Medora and Deadwood; reward for information on theft of its stock.
Milwaukee Beer by the case, keg or car load — C. B. Williams & Co., Bismarck, Dak.
E. J. Owenhouse, Bozeman, Mont. — stock saddles, Concord harness, fancy bits and spurs, chaparejos, reatas, quirts, hackamores.
Minneapolis & St. Louis R'y and the "Famous Albert Lea Route" — map and route to Chicago and St. Louis.
Wise & Goodkind, Bismarck, Dak. — wholesale dealers in wines, liquors, cigars; case & bar goods a specialty.
Brand: Medora Stage & F. Co., A. T. Packard, Gen. Mgr., Medora — horse brand cross-Y on left shoulder; horses on stations between Medora and Deadwood.
Brand: E. W. Casey & Co., Frank S. Moore, Mgr., P.O. Medora — KC on left hip and shoulder (2nd brand without circle); range O'Donnell creek.
Brand: Sloping Bottom Ranch, Lloyd Roberts, Proprietor, P.O. Medora — on left hip; range Little Missouri 7 mi S of N.P.R.R.; horse brand on left shoulder.
Brand: Badger Cattle Company, Howard Eaton, Mgr., P.O. Medora — VI on left hip, horse brand same; range Beaver creek and Little Missouri river.
Brand: Dorr Clark, Spearfish, Dakota — VVV on left side; ear mark under-bit in left ear; range Belle Fourche.
Brand: Clark & Plum, Spearfish, Dakota — E6 on left side; ear mark left ear cropped; range Grand river; additional brands ZD, DZ, ZD (bar), circle cross; $100 reward for killing or driving stock from the VVV or E6 ranges.
Brand: H. R. Tarbell & Co., Medora, Dak. — horse brand H on left shoulder; range Davis creek and Little Missouri river.
Brand: W. N. Thompson & Co., Wm. Dantz, Mgr., P.O. Medora — TD on left hip; ear mark tip of left ear cut off square; additional brands quarter-circle diamond and T.
Brand: Lemoyne Cattle Co. (Limited), D. K. Wade, Mgr., Medora — LC on left side and reversed C on right hip; range Little Missouri south of the R.R.; ranch Tepee bottom; horse brand LC; owners of DW brand.
Brand: Soho Cattle Co., P.O. Medora — SO on left side; ear marks swallow fork right, crop left; range Little Missouri river and Beaver creek, north of N.P.R.R.
Brand: N. P. Refrigerator Car Co., Medora, Dak. — several brands on left side including JP-style and cross-Y marks, horse brands the same; also steers bought of Mason & Lovell; calf mark left ear grubbed; ranges Little Missouri river and Beaver creek.
Brand: Spring Creek Ranch, L. D. & B. Rumsey, J. L. Truscott, Mgr., P.O. Medora — R on left hip; ears swallow forked; range south of N.P.R.R. on Little Missouri river.
Brand: Berry, Boice & Co., P.O. Keith, Montana — 777 on right hip, side and shoulder; ear mark grub the right ear; range south of N.P.R.R. on Little Missouri and Beaver creek.
Brand: E. G. Paddock, P.O. Medora — six-inch circle-dot on both sides; range six miles north of N.P.R.R. crossing of Little Missouri; horse brand four-inch circle-dot on left shoulder and hip.
Brand: Pennell & Roberts, P.O. Medora — RR on shoulder for horses and mules; a JP horse brand on left thigh (same block, apparently); ranch four miles down river from N.P.R.R. crossing.
Brand: Lydia S. Fuller, Frank S. Moore, Mgr., P.O. Medora — LSF on left shoulder; range O'Donnell creek.
Brand: Custer Trail Cattle Co., F. Alden Eaton, Supt., P.O. Medora — HK in circle on left side and other brands; horse brand TV on left hip; range Little Missouri river, Davis creek [and others, partly illegible].
Brand: Towers & Gudgell, P.O. Keith, Montana — OX on right side, additional V; range south of N.P.R.R. on Little Missouri river and Beaver creek.
Brand: Bad Lands Cattle Co., M. Wadsworth, Mgr., P.O. Medora — 7L, bellows and Pd brands; range Little Missouri river, fifteen miles north of Medora.
Brand: Neimmela Ranch, Gregor Lang, Mgr., P.O. Medora — thistle on left or right shoulder; range Keogh crossing of Little Missouri to Pretty butte; 2nd and 3rd brands (figure-eight style marks).
